This article shows how to carry imputation uncertainty into a downstream
model: impute the missing cells `m` times, fit the same model to each
completed dataset, and combine the fits. The code examples are not run during
site builds because posterior sampling can take several minutes. A successful
site build therefore does not verify that these examples run.

> **Read this before using pooled estimates.** The posterior route is
> implemented for a narrow set of analyses, but the registered validation
> found no supported result in 44 tested inferential rows: 12 failed and 32
> were indeterminate (the simulations were too imprecise to decide whether
> their criteria were met). These rows include complete-data controls and cover
> only the frozen simulation settings. Within that total, five of eight
> posterior slope regimes failed and three were indeterminate. Software
> eligibility is not evidence that an analysis is validated. See the
> [registered inferential results](validation-results.html#inferential-results).

## Which imputations can be pooled

### Choose a route

- **You want to fit a downstream model to several completed datasets.** If
  continuous traits are missing, the posterior route may be eligible only
  with one row per species, no covariates, and an analysis meeting the
  conditions below. Its inferential validity has not been established.
- **One continuous predictor is missing, while the outcome and other model
  variables are complete.** If missingness is at random (MAR), see the
  separate experimental [`multi_impute_analysis()` route
  documentation](../reference/multi_impute_analysis.html). Its eligibility
  rules differ from those for posterior draws.
- **You want to explore spread around point predictions.** Conformal or
  MC-dropout draws are for prediction diagnostics, not downstream inference;
  `with_imputations()` refuses them for that purpose.

The registered validation did not establish reliable downstream inference
for either route in the tested settings. These are different workflows with
different requirements.

`multi_impute()` offers three ways to draw the missing cells. The default,
`draws_method = "auto"`, uses `"posterior"` when the trait types and supplied
arguments fit that method (below). If they do not, it falls back to
`"conformal"` with a message explaining why. Inputs that cannot be imputed,
such as data with no missing cells or fewer than two observed values for a
trait, produce an error instead of a fallback.

| `draws_method` | What these draws provide | Can the software fit and combine them? |
|---|---|---|
| `"posterior"` | Posterior draws for eligible continuous traits; inferential validity is not established | Yes; software does not check whether your analysis formula meets the conditions below |
| `"conformal"` (`"auto"` fallback) | Show spread around point predictions for exploration; not for downstream inference | No; `with_imputations()` rejects these draws |
| `"mc_dropout"` | Show spread around point predictions for exploration; not for downstream inference | No; `with_imputations()` rejects these draws |

The conformal and MC-dropout draws perturb each missing cell around a point
prediction. They do not draw the cells jointly from their distribution given
the observed data. In the conformal route, continuous, count, ordinal, and
proportion traits use the reported `pred$se` as a scale input for fallback draws
when no finite conformal score is available. For log-transformed continuous
traits, log1p-transformed counts, and
logit-transformed proportions, `pred$se` is reported on the original scale, but
the draw is made on the transformed scale. Pigauto does not fully convert
`pred$se` between these scales, so diagnostic draw spread may be too wide or
too narrow. Fitted point predictions are unchanged. In a simulation of a
phylogenetic regression slope (16 regimes: two traits,
n = 300 or 1000, Pagel's lambda 1 or 0.5, random or
clade-structured missingness, 120 replicates each), conformal draws biased
the pooled slope towards zero by 0.20 to 0.46 and the pooled 95% intervals
covered the true slope in 0 to 17% of replicates. Other estimands were not
measured. `with_imputations()` therefore refuses these draws. A list of fits
built by hand is still pooled by `pool_mi()`, with a warning that its
provenance cannot be checked; do not do this with conformal or MC-dropout
draws.

This applies to the draws, not to the per-cell conformal intervals that
`impute()` reports. Those intervals summarise uncertainty about a single
imputed value and were close to 95% coverage in simulation (0.954 to 0.971,
GNN off, random missingness), but coverage can fall below 95% at small n
(about 100 species) and when missingness is clustered in clades.

`draws_method = "posterior"` fits a Bayesian multivariate phylogenetic mixed
model and samples each completed dataset from the posterior predictive
distribution of the missing cells. It currently requires:

- continuous traits only,
- one row per species (no `species_col`),
- no `covariates`,
- at least one missing cell and at least two observed values for each trait.

For the documented downstream route, the model must be linear in the imputed
traits on the scale used for imputation, and it must use only those traits.
For example, do not add an external covariate, a squared trait, or an
interaction. `with_imputations()` runs your fitting function on each completed
dataset and returns the fits. `pool_mi()` combines fixed-effect estimates and
their uncertainty across successful fits. Neither function checks whether the
model formula meets these conditions. Passing the software checks does not
establish that the analysis meets them or that its inference is validated.

### Evidence and limits

These results come from separate simulation campaigns and answer related,
distinct questions. The earlier campaign estimates coverage under its listed
conditions. The later registered campaign applies prespecified support
criteria across a broader, frozen set of scenarios. Read each result within
its own scope; for the current inferential evidence, see the
[registered results](validation-results.html#inferential-results).

**Later rerun of the earlier simulation campaign.** With pigauto's
separation prior, continuous traits, 30% missing completely at random, 200
datasets per condition, n = 100 to 1000, Pagel's lambda 0.3 to 1, and trait
correlation 0 or 0.5, Rubin-pooled downstream PGLS slopes and phylogenetic
correlations had 95% interval coverage from 0.925 to 0.975 across the tested
conditions. At lambda = 1 and trait correlation = 0.5, pigauto slope coverage
was 0.955, 0.940, and 0.965 at n = 100, 300, and 1000. At n = 100, pigauto's
slope bias relative to the complete-data estimate was about -0.037; the
matched frequentist multiple-imputation comparator had bias about -0.021.
These results describe this simulation, not general calibration.

**Later registered validation.** Across 44 tested inferential rows, none was
supported: 12 failed and 32 were indeterminate. This includes complete-data
controls and is limited to the frozen simulation settings. Within those
results, five of eight posterior slope regimes failed and three were
indeterminate, with empirical 95% coverage from 86.2% to 95.2%. See the
[registered inferential results](validation-results.html#inferential-results)
for scope and criteria.

**Sampler details.** The current separation prior uses half-Cauchy priors for
residual standard deviations, scaled to the observed latent traits, and an
LKJ(1) prior for the full residual-correlation matrix. Before applying the
numerical cutoff, the LKJ(1) prior does not give each pairwise correlation a
uniform distribution when there are more than two traits. For numerical
stability, the sampler gives zero prior density if the smallest eigenvalue of
the residual covariance matrix, standardized by observed latent-trait
standard deviations, is below 0.000001. In plain language, on this
standardized scale, variance along every unit-length direction must be at
least 0.000001. This cutoff narrows the prior support. Before pigauto 0.11.0.9002,
the
sampler used an inverse-Wishart residual prior. In the earlier campaign, that
legacy prior attenuated the relationship between correlated traits at lambda
near 1 (coverage 0.75 at n = 1000). It remains selectable only when
reproducing that analysis: set
`posterior_control = list(residual_prior = "iw")`. New posterior fits use the
separation prior described above by default.

As a separate, experimental option, `multi_impute_analysis()` declares the
substantive analysis model and supports one incomplete double-precision
continuous covariate under missing at random (MAR); the outcome and all other
analysis variables must be fully observed. Current supported models are a
Gaussian `lm`, binomial-logit `glm`, or Gaussian `lmer` with one random
intercept. Validity also depends on a correctly specified conditional
imputation model. For the binomial-logit `glm` (SMCFCS) and Gaussian `lmer`
(`jomo`) routes, inspect the engine's convergence diagnostics yourself:
pigauto captures engine warnings and stops if either route emits them, but it
does not calculate or certify sampler convergence. The Gaussian `lm` route
uses a separate Bayesian Normal-regression sampler. This route does not use
pigauto's phylogenetic baseline or GNN and does not propagate posterior-tree
uncertainty. See the [documented conditions for
`multi_impute_analysis()`](../reference/multi_impute_analysis.html). This
experimental route does not validate the posterior-draw route described
above.

## Impute

The bundled AVONET300 data are complete for the four continuous traits, so
we delete some values to have something to impute.

```{r impute}
library(pigauto)
data(avonet300, tree300)

traits <- avonet300[, c("Mass", "Wing.Length",
                        "Beak.Length_Culmen", "Tarsus.Length")]
rownames(traits) <- avonet300$Species_Key

set.seed(1)
traits$Mass[sample(nrow(traits), 60)] <- NA
traits$Wing.Length[sample(nrow(traits), 45)] <- NA

mi <- multi_impute(traits, tree300, m = 20L,
                   draws_method = "posterior", seed = 1L)
mi
```

With the default sampler settings, one sampler run for a simulated
four-trait dataset of 300 species took about ten minutes on one core (median
616 s, Totoro server). That run produces all `m` completed datasets; the time
is not ten minutes for each dataset. Fits that need automatic chain extensions
take longer. Check
convergence before using the draws: `mi$posterior$diagnostics`
holds split R-hat and bulk effective sample size for the monitored covariance
and lambda parameters. `multi_impute()` warns if the chains have not converged
after its automatic extensions. If the convergence flag is `FALSE` or
unavailable, stop before
interpreting or pooling these draws. Inspect the reported diagnostics and the
sampler controls in the [`multi_impute()` reference](../reference/multi_impute.html),
then refit and check again. Passing the sampler's convergence rule does not
establish calibrated downstream inference.

```{r diagnostics}
mi$posterior$diagnostics
attr(mi$posterior$diagnostics, "converged")
```

`mi$datasets` is a list of `m` completed data frames with species as row
names. Observed values are unchanged in every dataset; only the missing
cells differ.

## Fit and pool

`with_imputations()` applies a model-fitting function to every completed
dataset and attaches a workflow tag so pigauto can distinguish known
imputation routes. The tag does not check your model formula or independently
verify where the data came from. By default, a failed model fit is recorded
and reported while fitting continues; `pool_mi()` drops failed fits. Check the
failed dataset indices and the number of fits left before interpreting pooled
results. At least two successful fits are required. `pool_mi()` combines the
fixed-effect estimates with Rubin's rules (Rubin 1987; Barnard and Rubin 1999)
and returns one row per coefficient with the pooled estimate, standard error,
degrees of freedom, confidence interval and the fraction of missing
information (`fmi`).

`drmTMB` and `gllvmTMB` are optional model packages, not pigauto dependencies.
Install either separately before running its example: use
`install.packages("drmTMB")` for the location-scale model, or
`remotes::install_github("itchyshin/gllvmTMB")` for the latent-variable model.
Other external model packages used below also need to be installed separately.

The examples below show how each model class is fitted and how its fixed
effects are extracted. The registered posterior tests did not establish
calibrated inference: five of eight slope regimes failed and three were
indeterminate. The documented software route is limited to analyses linear
in the imputed continuous traits on the scale where they were imputed,
using variables among those traits. Check which traits `log_transform`
transformed before fitting `log(...)`. The joined diet variable,
distributional model, and latent-model structure in later examples are
compatibility demonstrations only. They are outside the documented posterior
inference eligibility conditions as well as the tested slope scenarios. Do
not treat those examples as supported downstream inference workflows.


The regression examples ask how wing length scales with body mass. The
latent-variable example is separate: it demonstrates pooling trait means
from a joint multivariate model.

### Phylogenetic regression (nlme)

By default, `multi_impute()` logs each continuous trait whose observed values
are all positive, then returns completed data on the original scale. In this
example, the `log(...)` formula uses the scale on which those traits were
imputed. If your input columns already contain logged values, set
`log_transform = FALSE` and use those columns directly in the model, for
example `Wing.Length ~ Mass`; wrapping them in `log()` would log them again.

```{r gls}
fits <- with_imputations(mi, function(d) {
  d$species <- rownames(d)
  nlme::gls(log(Wing.Length) ~ log(Mass), data = d,
            correlation = ape::corBrownian(phy = tree300, form = ~species),
            method = "ML")
})
pool_mi(fits)
```

### Compatibility example: mixed models (lme4 and glmmTMB)

These examples add a diet effect after imputation. Diet is not part of the
posterior imputation model, so these fits are outside its documented
downstream-inference conditions.

Variables that were not imputed can be joined to each completed dataset
inside the fitting function. Here diet category (`Trophic.Level`) becomes a
random intercept.

```{r mixed}
add_diet <- function(d) {
  d$Trophic.Level <- avonet300$Trophic.Level[
    match(rownames(d), avonet300$Species_Key)]
  d
}

fits_lmer <- with_imputations(mi, function(d) {
  lme4::lmer(log(Wing.Length) ~ log(Mass) + (1 | Trophic.Level),
             data = add_diet(d))
})
pool_mi(fits_lmer)

fits_tmb <- with_imputations(mi, function(d) {
  glmmTMB::glmmTMB(log(Wing.Length) ~ log(Mass) + (1 | Trophic.Level),
                   data = add_diet(d))
})
pool_mi(fits_tmb)
```

For `glmmTMB` fits, `pool_mi()` pools the conditional (mean) model only;
zero-inflation and dispersion coefficients are not included.

A caveat on joined variables: the posterior imputation model conditions on
the imputed traits and the tree, not on `Trophic.Level`. When a variable
that matters for the analysis is left out of the imputation model, its
association with the imputed traits is weakened in the imputed cells.
Because the posterior route accepts continuous traits only, a categorical
variable such as diet cannot currently be added to the imputation model;
treat its estimated effects with this in mind. (Diet is also a small
grouping factor here, four levels, one of them with a single species, so
the random-intercept variance is poorly estimated.)

### Compatibility example: location-scale model (drmTMB)

This model estimates how residual spread changes with body mass, while the
imputation model assumes constant residual variance. This example demonstrates
software compatibility and falls outside the documented posterior-inference
conditions.

`drmTMB` models the mean and the residual standard deviation together.
`pool_mi()` pools both sets of fixed effects, labelled `mu:` and `sigma:`.
The posterior imputation model has a constant residual variance, so the
imputed cells carry no relationship between body mass and residual spread.
We expect this to weaken a pooled `sigma:` slope when many cells are
imputed; this has not been measured.

```{r drmtmb}
fits_drm <- with_imputations(mi, function(d) {
  drmTMB::drmTMB(drmTMB::bf(log(Wing.Length) ~ log(Mass),
                            sigma ~ log(Mass)),
                 data = d)
})
pool_mi(fits_drm)
```

### Compatibility example: latent-variable model (gllvmTMB)

This joint latent-variable model demonstrates software compatibility and
falls outside the documented posterior-inference conditions. `pool_mi()`
below combines its fixed trait means; it does not pool latent loadings or
variance components.

`gllvmTMB` fits all traits jointly in long format. `pool_mi()` pools its
fixed effects (here the trait means); latent loadings and variance
components are not pooled.

```{r gllvmtmb}
to_long <- function(d) {
  tr <- names(d)
  data.frame(species = factor(rep(rownames(d), times = length(tr))),
             trait   = factor(rep(tr, each = nrow(d)), levels = tr),
             value   = log(unlist(d, use.names = FALSE)))
}

fits_gllvm <- with_imputations(mi, function(d) {
  gllvmTMB::gllvmTMB(value ~ 0 + trait +
                       latent(0 + trait | species, d = 1, unique = FALSE),
                     data = to_long(d), trait = "trait", unit = "species",
                     family = gaussian(), REML = FALSE,
                     engine = "tmb", silent = TRUE)
})
pool_mi(fits_gllvm)
```

### Other models

For other model classes, pass extractor functions to `pool_mi()` through
`coef_fun` and `vcov_fun`, or a `tidy_fun` returning `term`, `estimate`
and `std.error`. The same named, finite fixed-effect terms must be
available across the retained fits; inspect reported fit failures before
using pooled estimates.

## Bayesian models: concatenate, do not pool

For eligible posterior imputations and a compatible Bayesian analysis,
combine the fits by giving posterior draws from each imputed dataset equal
representation in the combined sample. Check convergence for every fit before
combining. Concatenating draws describes the combining procedure; it does not
establish calibrated inference beyond the regimes reported above. The
eligibility limits for the imputation method still apply. `pool_mi()` refuses
`brmsfit` and `MCMCglmm` objects because they have posterior draws rather than
Rubin-pooled coefficient estimates.

With brms, `brm_multiple()` fits every completed dataset and combines the
draws for you:

```{r brms}
fit_b <- brms::brm_multiple(log(Wing.Length) ~ log(Mass),
                            data = mi$datasets, chains = 2, refresh = 0)
summary(fit_b)
```

Check convergence separately for each imputed dataset, following the current
[`brm_multiple()` diagnostics guidance](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/reference/brm_multiple.html).
The combined diagnostics can look poor because the imputed datasets have
different posterior distributions. Zhou and
Reiter (2010) found that posterior interval estimates from stacked draws could
be too narrow with `m = 5` and, in some settings, `m = 20` compared with
`m = 100`. Their results motivate checking posterior-draw pooling as `m`
increases, while recognizing that the suitable number of imputations may
differ by setting and pooling method. Check whether the posterior summaries
of interest change as `m` increases.

With MCMCglmm, fit each dataset and bind the fixed-effect samples:

```{r mcmcglmm}
fits_mc <- lapply(mi$datasets, function(d) {
  MCMCglmm::MCMCglmm(log(Wing.Length) ~ log(Mass), data = d, verbose = FALSE)
})
sol <- coda::as.mcmc(do.call(rbind, lapply(fits_mc, function(f) f$Sol)))
summary(sol)
```

## References

Barnard J, Rubin DB (1999). Small-sample degrees of freedom with multiple
imputation. *Biometrika* 86: 948-955.

Nakagawa S, Freckleton RP (2008). Missing inaction: the dangers of ignoring
missing data. *Trends in Ecology and Evolution* 23: 592-596.

Rubin DB (1987). *Multiple Imputation for Nonresponse in Surveys*. Wiley.

Zhou X, Reiter JP (2010). A note on Bayesian inference after multiple
imputation. *The American Statistician* 64: 159-163.
